recent_posts.title: Give LLMs objective feedback to evaluate their own work
recent_posts.summary: Working effectively with LLMs requires giving them objective ways to evaluate their own work. The key is providing quick feedback mechanisms that indicate success or failure and guide corrections when things go wrong. This mirrors human development workflows: write code, run tests/compiler, iterate based on feedback. Tools with clear error messages and minimal verbose output work best. Good practices like comprehensive test suites, strong type systems, and helpful compiler errors benefit both LLMs and human developers. By optimizing the feedback loop, you can safely auto-accept LLM actions and dramatically increase development velocity.

recent_posts.title: Agentic development basics
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on tutorial for learning AI-assisted development using Claude Code. The guide emphasizes starting with simple tasks, using version control, committing to not writing code manually during the learning phase, and working with Claude's plan mode for larger features. It walks through building a basic CLI task tracker, demonstrating how to review Claude's suggestions, iterate on plans, and handle failures. The approach focuses on understanding the tool's limitations through deliberate practice before advancing to more sophisticated techniques.

recent_posts.title: How to think about Gas Town
recent_posts.summary: Gas Town is a project using AI agents to autonomously complete software development tasks from bug trackers. The core concept is straightforward: workspaces contain projects with bug trackers, and AI agents work through these tasks independently. The project's unconventional terminology and presentation style serves as a filtering mechanism to attract like-minded experimenters while deterring casual observers. This approach challenges traditional software development assumptions, particularly around rigor and testing, as the industry grapples with AI's impact on development practices.

recent_posts.title: Getting started with Claude for software development
recent_posts.summary: Claude can be a valuable tool for software developers, but it requires intentional learning and practice, similar to mastering vim. Start by using Claude for read-only code analysis and conversations about your existing code before attempting code generation. Treat the AI like a respected coworker, ask it to review code, identify bugs, or evaluate refactoring decisions. Begin with the web interface or invest $20/month for Claude Code, which can analyze entire codebases. Focus on building comfort with asking questions and evaluating responses critically rather than expecting perfect solutions immediately.

recent_posts.title: Thirteen years of Rust and the birth of Rue
recent_posts.summary: Steve Klabnik reflects on 13 years of using Rust and announces Rue, a new programming language he's building as a hobby project. He discusses how AI tools like Claude have made solo language development more feasible without large teams or funding. The project is in early stages and intentionally kept as a personal endeavor rather than a community-driven effort.

recent_posts.title: I see a future in jj
recent_posts.summary: Steve Klabnik shares his decision to join ERSC, a new company building a developer collaboration platform on top of jj, a modern version control system. Drawing parallels to his early involvement with Rust, he explains why jj has strong potential: it offers incremental adoption over Git, has backing from Google with significant internal usage, features a dedicated team with deep source control expertise, and is building a passionate community. The post details his framework for evaluating promising technology projects through market fit, team strength, and user base potential.

recent_posts.title: Claude AI excels at assembly programming but struggles with TailwindCSS upgrades
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares contrasting experiences using Claude AI for coding tasks. Claude struggled repeatedly with upgrading TailwindCSS to version 4, failing multiple times despite it being a popular framework. However, Claude excelled at a complex assembly programming task, successfully implementing x86_64 code generation for ELF executables and autonomously debugging segmentation faults by analyzing instruction sizes and jump calculations. The author finds it surprising that Claude performed better on the more obscure assembly task than the common web development upgrade.

recent_posts.title: Is Rust faster than C?
recent_posts.summary: Comparing Rust and C performance is complex because 'all things being the same' is difficult to define. While both languages can achieve similar performance through inline assembly and compiler optimizations, they differ in default behaviors like struct field ordering, bounds checking, and safety guarantees. Rust's compile-time safety checks may lead developers to write different code patterns than in C, affecting runtime performance. Social factors also play a role, as developers may be more willing to write performance-oriented code in Rust due to its safety guarantees. Fundamentally, there's no inherent reason Rust cannot match C's performance capabilities.

recent_posts.title: I am disappointed in the AI discourse
recent_posts.summary: The writer expresses frustration with the polarized nature of AI discussions, highlighting how both supporters and critics often make exaggerated claims. They mention interacting with ChatGPT and finding discrepancies in public perceptions of its capabilities. They advocate for more balanced, fact-based discourse around AI and its ethical implications.

recent_posts.title: Rust 1.0, ten years later
recent_posts.summary: Reflecting on a decade since Rust 1.0's release, its transition from a hobby to a widely-adopted professional language is evident. The early days were fraught with uncertainty, but Rust has become integral to major industry projects. Despite challenges, the community has fostered a robust language with ongoing work to perfect it.
